title: A boy leaves the east
hookLine: Jalal al-Din is born around 1207 in the eastern Persian world, and his family walks west as the Mongols approach

cards: Packing up a whole life looks much the same in any century. Boxes, a cart or a truck, the house you grew up in shrinking behind you.

Now go back to around the year 1216, in the far east of the Persian-speaking world, near what is now northern Afghanistan. A respected preacher gathers his family, his books and his students, and starts walking west.
His little son is about nine. The boy's name is Jalal al-Din Muhammad. He will not come back.
Years later, when he's well-known, people will call him by the name of the place where he ended up.

teach.b: Tradition says Jalal al-Din was born in 1207 in Balkh, an old city of scholars. Some modern historians think it was really Vakhsh, a smaller town in today's Tajikistan, where his father was working at the time.
Either way, he was born in the eastern Persian world, and Persian was his language.

His father, Baha al-Din Walad, was a preacher and a teacher of religion, a serious man who wrote down his own inner life in a notebook the family kept. Somewhere between 1216 and 1220 the family set out.
The old accounts say they went ahead of the Mongols, whose armies swept through the region and wrecked Balkh around 1220. Some scholars add that Baha al-Din had quarrels at home too.
Nobody knows every reason, and the sources don't agree.
What's known is the road: Baghdad, a pilgrimage to Mecca, then years in towns across Anatolia, the land that is now Turkey. On the way the boy grew up, married young, and lost his mother.
Around 1228 the family settled in Konya. Now the surprise. Anatolia had once been part of the Roman Empire, so people in the east called it Rum, Rome.
A man from Rum was Rumi. The name English readers know him by comes from where he landed, not where he started.
Keep that road in mind all camp: being far from where you began comes back again and again in what you'll read.

how: Visitors from many countries travel to Konya, in Turkey, to the museum and tomb of Rumi, and his birthplace is honored in Afghanistan and Tajikistan as well; readers often start with the story of his family's long journey west.

o: an old city of scholars, by tradition his birthplace
the Anatolian city where Rumi's family finally settled
a Persian word for a traveler who leaves home

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.

s: his name was Jalal al-Din Muhammad. Rumi means from Rum, the old Roman land of Anatolia, where he settled.
we know exactly why the family left
the old accounts point to the Mongols; some scholars add quarrels at home. the sources don't agree.
he was born in the eastern Persian world and wrote most of his poetry in Persian.

games.q: you're Baha al-Din, around 1216. armies are coming from the east, and you have a family and a household of books. what do you do?
o: stay and hope the storm passes.
take the family and walk west.
send the boy alone to safety.
games.why: the family walks west together, through Baghdad and Mecca to Anatolia. Balkh was wrecked around 1220; the boy grew up on the road.

practice: Think of a place you left: a town, a house, a school, a country, a friendship. What did it smell like, what did the light do in the afternoon, who was there?
Don't judge whether leaving was right; just stand there again for a minute, then notice who you became because you left.

wordCard.voice: Balkh, the old city of scholars in today's Afghanistan where tradition says young Jalal al-Din was born. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the road west. Far from where he began, a boy grows up. See you in Konya tomorrow.
